newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's order grappling with succession.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's order grappling with succession.

text.p: More than 100 Roman Catholic nuns remained cloistered on Sunday in a search for their religious order's successor to Mother Teresa.
"Wait for a few more days, you will come to know," Sister Christine, a spokeswoman at the Missionaries of Charity, told Reuters.
Sources at the religious order said the delayed elections to find a successor to the ailing 86-year-old Roman Catholic nun would be completed by next week.
The order might opt to set up a committee of senior nuns to lead it rather than name just one successor to Mother Teresa, they said.

"This is the usual practice in big congregations who have a large number of workers," a senior church official said. "It is quite possible that this model will also be introduced by the Missionaries of Charity."
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, suffering from heart, kidney and lung ailments, has said she does not want to continue to lead the order she founded in 1948.
She went to hospital three times last year, and although she continues to work, she has lost some of her characteristic vigour, church officials said.
The election of Mother Teresa's successor has been postponed twice since September. It was first set for September 8, but put off because Mother Teresa was ill.
Senior nuns from around the world then went into retreat on January 16, confining themselves to their rooms in the order's headquarters in Calcutta to pray.

They had planned to vote in a secret ballot on February 2, after the two-week retreat. But the order's electoral college, apparently unable to find a clear-cut successor for the controversial Mother Teresa, decided instead to hold closed-door deliberations at the headquarters before holding a vote.
The election process involves the 132 members of the order's electoral order, or General Chapter, which represents the order's 4,500 nuns.
